text: I read your report over the weekend. It is fine, I guess. I did not have strong feelings about it either way. The topic is not one I know much about. Perhaps someone from the finance team should have a look at it as well. Let me know when you want to talk.
The report is too long. Please make it shorter and clearer. Then send it back to me.
Thank you for sending the draft. The layout is tidy and easy to follow. However, some parts are weak and need more work.
This draft is sloppy. I expected more from you. Do it again.
You were careless with the numbers and lazy with the summary. I am not happy about this, and I told you last time that I wanted a better result. Fix it before Friday.

The draft is weak and it feels rushed. I do not see why anyone should read it. The numbers are hard to trust, the tables are crowded, and the writing is uneven from one part to the next. Please improve it soon and tell me when it is done.

Thank you for sharing your report with me. I think it is a good start, and I can see that a lot of thought went into it. Keep going and it will get better. I would be happy to talk about it again once you have had time to think about the next version.

I appreciate the effort you put into this. The topic is interesting and relevant to what the team is doing this year. The tone is friendly and the ideas are mostly sensible. I hope the next version is a bit more polished, and I look forward to reading it.
Nice work on the whole. I enjoyed reading it. Thank you for the quick turnaround.

The report does not convince me. It feels incomplete, and I kept wondering what the point was meant to be. The opening promises a lot, and the middle says very little. By the end I had forgotten what the question was. I think you need to rethink the whole thing and start again from a clean sheet.
I did not like the conclusion because it felt rushed. The rest was okay. Please look at it again.

The summary is confusing. I got lost halfway through, and I had to start again from the top. The sentences are long, the headings are not helpful, and the order of the ideas seems random. Maybe ask someone else to read it too.
Check the table on page three. It looks wrong to me. Fix it.
The intro needs work. The ending is abrupt. The middle is fine.

Too many typos in the report. Please proofread it before it goes to anyone else. Some of the words are missing, some are doubled, and a few names are spelled in two different ways. I will read it again next week.

I have only skimmed it. It looks fine at first glance, and the layout is what I expected. I will read it properly when I have more time, which may not be before the end of the month. Send me the final version when it is ready, and tell me who else has seen it.
Thanks for the draft. It was a bit hard to follow. Perhaps simplify the structure.

The report needs more detail in places. I can see you tried, and I appreciate it. It was clearly written in a hurry, and a few of the choices you made were hard to follow. Keep at it, and let me know how it goes.
Thank you for the draft. The section on costs is unclear to me. Please rewrite it so that the numbers are easier to follow.

I appreciate the clear structure of the report. However, the section on risks is thin. For example, the second risk has no explanation at all. I suggest adding a short paragraph on how likely each risk is.

Thank you for the draft, and well done on the clear structure. The data in the figure on page four support your main point. However, the section on risks is thin, because the second risk is not explained at all. I suggest a short paragraph for each risk, for example one with the likely cost. Alternatively, you could use a small table instead.
Thanks for the report. I found it hard to see the main point. The ending could be stronger.

Nice work on the summary. The table on page two could be clearer, since the columns have no labels. Try adding a label to each column, for example the unit of measurement. However, the rest reads well.

Thank you for the draft, I appreciate the effort. The strength of the report is the clear data in the figure on page five. However, the section on staffing is thin because it gives no numbers. For example, you do not say how many people the project needs. I suggest adding a table, or alternatively a short paragraph with the headcount. This could also help the reader, since the budget depends on it.
The report is careless in places. The section on costs has several errors. Please check it again before you send it on.

The section on costs has errors, for example the total on page six does not match the table. This looks sloppy, so please check every figure again. Try to explain the method, because readers will ask how you got the numbers. Otherwise, the report is solid.

Thank you for the draft. The section on costs is the weakest part, because the totals on page six do not match the table. For example, the figure for travel is higher in the summary than in the detail. I suggest you check every number against the source data, since small errors damage trust in the whole report. Alternatively, ask a colleague to review the costs instead of doing it alone. However, the other sections are well done.

I appreciate how clear the introduction is. The methods section could use more detail, because I could not repeat the steps with the data you describe. Try listing the steps one by one, for example in a short table. Alternatively, add an appendix. However, overall this is a good draft.

Thank you for the draft, I appreciate the care you took. The strength of the report is the evidence in the figure on page three. However, the methods section is hard to repeat because some steps are missing. For example, you do not say how the sample was chosen. I suggest a short paragraph listing every step, or alternatively a small table. This could also answer the questions a reviewer is likely to raise, since they rely on the data.
The draft is okay. Thanks for sending it. I could not follow the argument in some places, and it needs work.

Your data analysis is strong. However, the section on limits is missing, which is careless, because readers need to know how far the data can be trusted. Please add it, for example after the results on page nine. I would try to keep it short.

Thank you for the draft. The analysis is the strength of the report, and the figure on page eight is clear. However, the section on limits is missing, because the results depend on one small sample. I suggest adding a short paragraph on this, for example after the table on page nine. Since the data are thin, you could also say what evidence would change your view.
The conclusion is too long. The recommendations are not clear to me. Cut it down and try again.
Thank you for the draft. The section on the market is useful. The tone is a little too formal for the board.
Nice work on the market section. However, the figure on page seven is hard to read, because the labels are small. I suggest larger labels, and you could add the source of the data below the figure.

I appreciate the effort, and the strength of the report is the evidence for the market size. However, the section on competitors is thin, since it names only one rival. For example, the table on page ten lists two more that you do not discuss. I suggest adding a paragraph on each, or alternatively a short comparison. This could make your case stronger, because the board will ask about them.

Thank you for the draft, and well done on the clear structure of section two. I appreciate the evidence: the figure on page three shows the trend and the data back it up. The section on costs needs work because the totals do not match the table, for example the travel line in the summary is higher than in the detail. I suggest checking each number against the source, or alternatively asking a colleague to review it. Since the board will read this closely, a short paragraph on how you built the estimate could be a real strength.

Your argument is easy to follow, and I appreciate the care in section three. The pricing claim on page five needs a source because the discount figure has none. Try adding the pilot data as evidence, in a short table or alternatively a paragraph. Well done on the summary, since it states the main point first.

Well done, and thank you for the early copy. Nice work on page three: the figure is clear evidence. Section four needs sources, because the claims cannot be checked. For example, the market line has no reference. Try a short paragraph for each claim, since that gives the reason. Another option is a table.

I appreciate the thorough draft, and the data are a real strength. The section on risks is thin because the numbers stop in March. Please add the latest figures, such as a table for each quarter, or alternatively a short paragraph. That could help the reader, since the risks change fast.

Nice work on the whole, and thank you for the care you took with section three. A real strength is the evidence behind the main claim: the figure on page four and the data in the table agree. The paragraph on cost savings is unclear, though, because the baseline is missing. For example, the line on savings per month does not say what it is compared with. I suggest adding the baseline, or alternatively a one-sentence reason for the comparison. The board will ask, so this could save you a long discussion.

I appreciate the thorough draft. The section on staffing on page eight needs a figure, because the text alone is hard to follow. A chart of headcount per team, such as the one in the annex, would help, and the data are ready.

Thank you for the draft, and well done on the clear summary. The evidence in the figure on page five is strong, but the section on timing is thin because it gives no dates. The line about the launch should name a month, and a short paragraph with the main dates would do, or alternatively a simple table.

Thank you for the draft, and I appreciate the honest tone, a real strength. The figure on page six is confusing since the axis has no label. Try adding the unit, for example weeks or months. The data are good evidence, and I suggest saying so, because the reason for the choice should show. Well done on section two.

Well done, and thank you for the quick turnaround. I appreciate the strength of the plan: the data on page three and the evidence in the annex agree. Section five should say why the second option was dropped, because the board may prefer it. Try a short table, because it shows the reason at a glance. The paragraph on cost, for example, does not compare the two options.

Thank you for the draft, I appreciate the effort. The evidence in the figure on page seven is a clear strength. The section on suppliers needs one more case, because the claim about delays rests on a single one. The claim about the March delivery could be backed by the data from other months, such as April. I suggest adding a short paragraph with those data, or alternatively a small table.
Nice work, and thank you for the clear draft. Section three is thin because it names no sources, so try adding them as a short paragraph at the end. The figure on page two is strong evidence.

Thank you for the early copy. I appreciate the strength of the plan, since the data on page nine are clear. The line for training, for example, has no breakdown. Try a table, because the reason for each cost should show. Section six could use one too.

Well done on the draft. Thank you for the early copy as well. The data in the figure on page four are clear evidence for your main point. The section on next steps is thin because it has no owners. The line on testing, for example, does not say who runs it. I suggest a name for each step, or alternatively a short paragraph on roles.

Thank you for the draft. A real strength of the report is the clear evidence in the figure on page five, and I appreciate the honest tone. Section six could explain the reason for the delay, since the board will ask. A short paragraph with the dates and the data would be enough for that, for example. I suggest this in place of the long footnote, because it is easier to find.

Nice work on the whole. The evidence on page three is strong, but the section on risks needs a source for the data, because I could not check the figure. You could add it below the table, since readers will look there first.

Thank you for the draft, and well done on the clear summary. What impressed me most is the evidence in the figure on page six, a clear strength. The section on costs is hard to check, because the totals have no source. For example, the line for travel could point to the data in the annex. I suggest adding the source after each total, or alternatively a short paragraph on the method.

I appreciate the care you took with section two, and the data in the figure on page three are good evidence. The paragraph on benefits is vague, since it gives no numbers. The line on faster delivery, for example, could name the days saved. Try adding the numbers, and consider a table instead of the paragraph. The reason is simple: a reader who checks the data will trust the plan.

Thank you for the draft. The data on page four are the strength of the report, and the figure is clear evidence. Section five could be shorter, because the same point appears twice. You could cut the second paragraph, for example the one on page eight.
